title: Kabir: the death that delights
hook: the death the world fears fills Kabir with joy, for it brings the Beloved near (Kabir salok, ang 1365)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's true warrior. Your line was fight for the helpless. Did you stand up for one small thing? Today, Kabir looks at the thing most people fear most, and smiles. Day two hundred fifty-six.

Most of us have a way of not talking about death. We change the subject. We say passed away, or lost, or gone. We don't put it on the calendar. And that's human; it's a frightening thing. Now picture an old weaver who, when the subject comes up, doesn't flinch. He leans in. He says the thing everyone's afraid of makes his heart glad. Not because he's tired of life. Because of who he thinks is waiting. Today, Kabir: the death that delights.
screen: `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `ONE WEAVER LEANS IN.` → `HIS HEART IS GLAD.`

segments.voice: Among Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1365, is this one: kabeer jis marne te jag darai mere man aanand; marne hee te paaeeai pooran parmaanand. Kabir, the death the world is so afraid of fills my mind with bliss; for it's through dying that one finds perfect, supreme joy. Aanand is joy, the same word as the Anand Sahib. Parmaanand is supreme joy. So why joy? Remember the bride from ten days ago, waiting for her beloved, and Sohila's wedding date, already written. Kabir stands in that same picture. If the soul is a bride longing for God, then the day of meeting isn't a disaster. It's the day she's been waiting for. There's a second layer. Kabir, and the Gurus after him, often speak of dying while alive: letting the ego die, the proud little I we called haumai. In another salok, in paraphrase, Kabir says the whole world keeps dying, yet nobody knows how to die; die the kind of death after which you never die again. Many read that as the death of ego, which frees a person to live without fear. Tradition adds a story people tell. In old Benares, many believed that dying in the holy city brought liberation, and dying in the town of Maghar did not. Kabir, it's said, went to Maghar to die, to show that it's the heart, not the place. His own hymns say Kashi and Maghar are the same to one who has God in the heart.
screen: `WHAT THE WORLD FEARS, KABIR WELCOMES.` · `AANAND — THE BRIDE'S JOY.` · `DIE BEFORE YOU DIE: THE EGO.` · `KASHI OR MAGHAR — THE SAME.` · then, large: `WHAT THEY FEAR, I WELCOME.`

segments.voice: This one asks for a little courage, and it's gentle. Sit comfortably. Let yourself remember, quietly, that one day this breath will be the last one. Notice whatever comes up, fear, sadness, or calm, and don't push it away. Then notice this breath, now, which is here. And the next. For a minute, sit without fear, or with fear sitting beside you, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. Here, his salok: the death the world fears fills his heart with joy, for through it comes supreme bliss, the meeting with the Beloved.
Your line: what they fear, I welcome. Today, when a small fear comes, of a call, a change, a no, meet it for one breath instead of running. Day two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Kabir's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and often quoted at Sikh funerals and in reflections on death, where Sikh teaching discourages loud mourning and speaks of death as the soul's return.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aanand, joy; the same word as the Anand Sahib, and here, Kabir's joy at meeting death.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy man should be serious and sad about death.
what it means: if the soul is a bride going to her beloved, death is the meeting; and dying to ego frees a person to live without fear.
what a scholar hears: Salok Kabir, Ang 1365; aanand and parmaanand; the Maghar story is hagiographic, but Kabir's own hymns in the Granth reject the idea that Kashi grants liberation.
